Albanese 'limited' in cost-of-living relief he can offer
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is taking questions now and is asked about the upcoming mid-year budget update.
He says the government is limited in what it can do to provide Australians with cost-of-living relief as inflation remains a persistent problem.
But the freezing the cost of PBS-listed medicines at $25 is "targeted".
The PM insists there will be "substantial savings" found in the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.
Asked about the cost of the extension, Health Minister Mark Butler puts the price tag at $242m over three years. That takes us to the end of the decade.
Freezing scripts at $25 'sends right message': Pharmacy Guild
An extension of a PBS medicines freeze will keep the cost of a script at 2004-levels until the end of the decade, Health Minister Mark Butler says.
"This is a really important measure. It's going to help with the hip pocket, but it's also going to help build a healthier Australia," he says.
Butler says pharmacists have told him stories of customers asking what medications they could go without because of cost-of-living pressures.
Pharmacy Guild of Australia VP Simon Blacker says the move "sends the right message to patients across Australia".

"We have patients juggling things like rent, mortgage repayments, fuel, groceries. But what they can do over the next few years now is know that the price of those medicines are not going to change at all," he says.
Albanese announces PBS medication to stay at $25 until 2030
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirms the government will move to freeze the cost of PBS medicines at $25 until 2030.

"This helps Australians with the cost of medicines but it helps to keep our nation heathier as well. And we understand the cost of essential medicines can put pressure on household budgets and that's why we're giving Australians access to cheaper medicines," he says.
He confirms legislation will be introduced to parliament this morning.
Anthony Albanese is speaking now
Surprise! We have an early morning press conference from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to get us started.

Usually, his preference is to hold these press conferences in his prime ministerial courtyard. But it's raining at the moment in Canberra, so he's been forced indoors to the Blue Room (named so because of its blue colour scheme).
Albanese enters with Health Minister Mark Butler.
Hume hopeful gas reservation deal can be struck this week
OK, we've got a press conference from Anthony Albanese within the next couple of minutes.
So I'm gong to speedrun you through what Jane Hume had to say about a number of key bills being negotiated in the Senate.

Hume says the gas reservation scheme, which would force Australia's largest gas exports to save up to 20 per cent of supply for the domestic market, is something the Coalition wants, but not "at any price".
She calls the carve-out for WA a "significant move and a good first start" but there is "more to be done".
"I hope that we do [get a deal done] but … the ball is in the government's court," she says.

When it comes to the digital duty of care, the Coalition has already declared it won't support the legislation. Asked if the government's exemption of small business websites addressed the opposition's concerns, Hume says it doesn't.

"It's still a blank check for censorship, particularly political censorship. It gives the government and the eSafety Commissioner sweeping powers over what are very vague and subjective definitions of what online harm is," she says.
Bowen 'failed' at COP31: Hume
Liberal frontbencher Jane Hume has placed the blame for a breakdown in COP31 talks squarely on Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.
Debate broke down at the climate conference after the deal put forward by presidents Australia and Türkiye was rejected after the draft failed to mention fossil fuels.
Hume tells ABC Radio National Breakfast it was "extraordinary" for the summit to end without a deal and that Bowen had failed.

"Not only has he failed in these negotiations as the lead negotiator, but he has also failed Australians at the time when he spent $150 million just to be there, just to get this presidency in the first place," he says.
Watt defends Bowen after COP talks fail
Labor frontbencher Murray Watt is first up in the ABC Radio National Breakfast hot seat and faces questions about the breakdown of talks at COP31.
Watt doesn't think the result means Australia failed. Rather, it shows how hard it is to bridge the gap between nations on climate and energy policy.
"Obviously agreement was not able to be reached across what are some very divergent interests," he says.

"You know, I think what this shows is a very challenging international environment, at the moment, to reach agreement on almost anything and particularly a situation like this, where you've got fossil fuel producers on the one hand and other countries that are experiencing very serious impacts from climate change."
Watt notes that the US didn't send an official delegation to Antayla.
He said a range of nations were not prepared to sign the draft agreemeent if fossil fuels were included in it, but the opposite was true for others.
"This is the difficulty you've got when you've got different groups taking very, very different positions," Watt says.
Bowen surely 'frustrated' after breakdown of COP31 talks: Plibersek
Labor's Tanya Plibersek was also asked to give her reaction to the breakdown in talks at the UN COP summit.

"It's frustrating that we didn't get further. I'm sure [Climate Change and Energy Minister] Chris [Bowen] is the most frustrated person I can think of right now because he put many hours ... into these negotiations and really wanted to see something of an improvement on where we are now globally," she tells Seven.
"But there's no country that can do this on its own and without coming together we can't advance those talks."
One Nation recruit Barnaby Joyce, who was also on the panel, criticised Bowen for focusing on a "plenary session in Antalya" rather than small businesses and pensioners.
"Worry about happens in the kitchen table room in Australia. That's what he should be worrying about, the people who can't pay their power bills, the families can't afford to get ahead," he says.
The pair's appearance then descended into a shouting match (as they often do) about the cost of Labor and One Nation's climate and energy policies.
Outcome of COP31 talks 'disappointing': Ayres
Labor frontbencher Tim Ayres says the breakdown of talks at COP31 is a "disappointing outcome".
Ayres says the government will "keep on keeping on".
"Obviously it's disappointing. These multilateral conferences require consensus. That is, every country has to agree, or at the very least don't disagree, to the final outcome," he tells Nine.
"We will keep on keeping on, building on the frameworks that are established in the future to develop the response."
But Michaelia Cash, who was also on the morning television panel, didn't agree.
She placed the blame squarely on Chris Bowen, who served as the president of negotiations, who she criticised for focusing on COP rather pressures at home.

"Whilst Australians are doing it tough at home and living an economic nightmare … Chris Bowen was overseas negotiating for countries like Australia to spend billions more in providing international climate financing."
COP31 ends without deal after climate change talks break down
The COP31 UN climate summit has ended without a deal after debate broke down over a draft which failed to mention fossil fuels.

The main deal was rejected on Sunday afternoon, local time, by a host of nations, 44 hours after the summit's official close and following two weeks of negotiations. It marked the longest UN climate summit ever.

In a chaotic finale to the talks in the Turkish city of Antalya, debate continued in overtime until COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye confirmed they would not put forward another draft of the deal.

Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that did not mention fossil fuels, slamming it as too weak.

"We will not endorse a cover decision … that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.
Key Event
Government confirms small business websites will be exempt from digital duty of care

Yesterday the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry voiced concerns that small businesses may be caught up in the government's digital duty of care bill, which would require companies to prevent harm on their online platforms.
ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar said businesses were unsure what steps they needed to take to comply with the laws.

"A small business should not have to engage lawyers simply to work out whether its website is caught by a regime carrying penalties of more than $100 million. The answer should be in black and white in the legislation," McKellar said.
But in a statement, Wells confirmed small businesses will be exempt.
"A low-risk website for a cafe or bookkeeper is unlikely to cause harm to its users so, once the Digital Duty of Care starts, they will be exempt from the law," she said.

"The intention of the Digital Duty of Care is to put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur — not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses."
Key Event
Greens 'optimistic' on passing digital duty of care laws this week
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says she is "working hard" to try and get a deal done on the government's digital duty of care bill before the end of the week.
The Albanese government is hoping to pass the laws — which would put an onus on big tech companies to prevent foreseeable harms online — before parliament wraps up for the year.
But they'll need the Greens' support to do so.
Hanson-Young says she is "optimistic" about her conversations with the government, including on the Greens' non-negotiable amendment to enable Australians to sue tech companies if they are harmed.
"I'm hopeful that we are getting somewhere with the government on this," she said.
"We've seen them open to door to allowing for individuals and organisations to take big tech to court."
Hanson-Young says "the ball is in the government's court" to deliver amendments that will strengthen the laws.
"If we can come to an agreement, that is great. If it has to wait until next year, so be it."
Good morning 👋
Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

It's the final sitting week of the year, can you believe it? The parliament (well, the Senate) will have a busy week as it tries to land a deal on several bills the government wants passed by the end of the week.
From the gas reservation scheme, digital duty of care, trusts and the capital gains discount, and private health insurance, there's still a lot to resolve before MPs fly home for the year.

In addition to all of that, Foreign Minister Penny Wong is expected to this week elevate AI as a national security challenge. Elsewhere, the government is still insisting all is fine with AUKUS. More on both of those stories shortly.
